html:
Fiji is a group of more than 300 islands in Melanesia, in the South Pacific. The map shows it from 1880 to 2010. People first arrived about 3,000 years ago with the Lapita culture. Fijian society later mixed Melanesian and Polynesian ways, with close ties to Tonga (Tuʻi Tonga maritime network).

In the early 1800s traders came for sandalwood and then sea cucumbers, bringing muskets that sharpened wars between chiefs. The chief Seru Epenisa Cakobau was proclaimed king of Fiji in 1871, and in 1874 he and other chiefs handed the islands to Britain (England, then Britain). The next year a measles epidemic killed perhaps a third of the Fijian people.

The first British governor kept most land in Fijian hands and ruled through the chiefs. To grow sugar, the colony brought in workers from India (Indian indenture in Fiji) from 1879 to 1916. Their descendants, the Indo-Fijians, came to make up about half the population.

Fiji became independent in 1970. Tension between the two communities led to the military coups of 1987 and further coups in 2000 and 2006. Many Indo-Fijians have since emigrated.
